children: Industry representatives flag import dependence, renewable power costs and financing gaps as India targets a nearly threefold increase in steelmaking capacity by 2047

India’s proposed expansion of steelmaking capacity to 604 million tonnes (MT) by 2047 will depend on securing raw materials, managing power costs and cutting emissions without making steel unaffordable, industry representatives have said in responses to the draft National Steel Policy Vision 2047. The draft, released by the Ministry of Steel for public consultation in October 2026, envisages crude steel capacity rising from about 220 MT to 604 MT.

It projects finished steel demand of 505 MT, per capita consumption of 302 kg and exports of 45 MT by 2047. The expansion would require around 18 MT of additional capacity every year for 21 years, while reducing emissions intensity from 2.54 tonnes of carbon dioxide per tonne of crude steel to 1.54 tonnes. The industry inputs underline a central tension: India must add capacity without deepening its dependence on imported coking coal or locking in carbon-intensive production.

Sureshbabu Chigurupalli, Vice-President and Head of the Ferro Alloys Business Unit at Indian Metals & Ferro Alloys Ltd (IMFA), identified coking coal dependence as a major risk. India imports around 92 per cent of the coking coal it uses, while demand is projected to rise from 72 MT to 236 MT by 2047. “That level of import dependence leaves the industry exposed to price volatility and supply disruption,” Chigurupalli said. He added that iron ore, logistics infrastructure and skilled capacity must expand alongside steelmaking.

He also cautioned that the 300 MT capacity target set under the 2017 policy for 2030 remained unmet. The policy analysis estimates iron ore requirements at about 772 MT by 2047. Raw materials account for 65–70 per cent of steelmaking costs, making supply security and efficiency important to the affordability of steel for infrastructure, construction, automobile and engineering industries.

Pranav Bansal, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Bansal Wire Industries Limited, said crude steel production reached 168.4 MT in financial year 2025–26, highlighting the scale of expansion required. India imported 66.33 MT of coking coal in FY26, he noted. “Steel-price volatility and fluctuating raw-material costs make efficient procurement and working-capital management critical, particularly for MSMEs,” Bansal said. He pointed to automation, productivity and technology adoption as ways to improve manufacturers’ competitiveness.

The draft seeks to reduce emissions intensity by about 39 per cent. The policy analysis says around 2,550 secondary steel producers account for nearly 47 per cent of India’s capacity, making their transition important to meeting the target. Vaibhav Kakulte, President, Business Development and Corporate Relations at Greta Energy, said electric arc furnaces could lower emissions, particularly when powered by renewable electricity and supplied with more scrap.

However, he cautioned that “round-the-clock industrial operations require reliable power”, while renewable procurement, storage, transmission and open-access costs can affect project economics. Kakulte called for predictable open-access and banking arrangements, stronger transmission connectivity, long-tenure finance and targeted technology support for secondary steel producers. He also described coal gasification as a potential source of syngas for direct reduced iron production, while saying its decarbonisation contribution would depend on lifecycle emissions, coal quality, process efficiency and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.

Chigurupalli called for efficiency upgrades, waste-heat recovery and renewable power in the near term, alongside funded programmes for green hydrogen and carbon capture. He said smaller producers would need financial and technical support. Bansal said India’s Green Steel Taxonomy could help promote lower-emission production, while research, specialised steel manufacturing and domestic supplier development would be essential. The policy analysis warns that lower emissions per tonne may not translate into lower overall emissions as production rises.

It estimates that producing around 500 MT of steel at 1.54 tonnes of CO₂ per tonne could generate about 770 million tonnes of CO₂, compared with roughly 430 million tonnes at current production and intensity. India’s steel transition will therefore be judged not only by the capacity it adds, but by whether it can secure supplies, contain costs and reduce the sector’s total carbon footprint.
